I study how disaster risk emerges from interactions among natural hazards, infrastructure systems, and human decision-making, developing computational frameworks under deep uncertainty that link hazard physics with the natural, built, and social systems shaping risk.
Currently, I am a Postdoctoral Researcher at the NSF-funded Coastal Hazards, Economic Prosperity, and Resilience (CHEER) Hub within the Disaster Research Center. Working with Dr. Rachel Davidson and Dr. Linda Nozick, I focus on integrating hazard processes, built environment, human behavior, and policy decisions into unified modeling frameworks to understand how interventions shape long-term risk and resilience.
I earned my Ph.D. in Industrial Engineering from Purdue University, advised by Dr. David Johnson. My doctoral work developed adaptive infrastructure strategies using reinforcement learning and belief updating for decision-making under deep uncertainty, and contributed to the risk assessment models used in Louisiana’s $50 billion Comprehensive Master Plan for a Sustainable Coast.
My work has been recognized through research awards, competitive funding, and professional leadership. I have served as Chair of the Engineering and Infrastructure Specialty Group of the Society for Risk Analysis, and was named an NSF Ocean Decade Champion. I have also received recognition for my research on adaptive decision-making under uncertainty.




Jul 2026 — Our work on multi-stakeholder risk and land-use planning will be presented at the 13th U.S. National Conference on Earthquake Engineering (13NCEE), Portland, OR, examining how development dynamics reshape long-term disaster risk.
May 2026 — Research spotlight presentation at the NHERI Computational Symposium on computational methods for modeling long-term sequences of hazard losses and their implications for recovery and resilience.
Mar 2026 — Two first-authored papers accepted:

Stakeholder Dynamics in Disaster Mitigation Funding (International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction)
Optimization-Based Event-Loss Scenario Generation (Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in Engineering Systems)

Dec 2025 — Presented first-authored research at the Society for Risk Analysis Annual Meeting on how land-use planning and multi-stakeholder dynamics shape disaster risk and its distribution.

text: My research develops computational frameworks for understanding disaster risk as a coupled human–natural system, supporting decision-making under deep uncertainty. I integrate hazard modeling, dynamic exposure, and multi-stakeholder behavior to evaluate how policies shape both total risk and its distribution.

title: Research
text:
Multi-Stakeholder Dynamics
Risk is shaped not only by hazards, but by how households, insurers, and governments respond and interact over time. This work develops multi-stakeholder modeling frameworks to evaluate how mitigation funding, insurance pricing, and household decisions jointly shape long-term disaster outcomes.


Stakeholder-based framework linking hazard, exposure, and decision-making across households, insurers, and governments.



Policy design space illustrating how timing, spatial scale, and allocation rules shape mitigation outcomes.


Key idea: Stakeholder interactions determine how risk is distributed and how mitigation benefits are realized.

title: Research
text:
Hazard & Loss Modeling
Disaster outcomes begin with how hazard events are represented and translated into long-term loss. This work develops computationally efficient methods for representing multi-decade hazard-loss sequences while preserving temporal, probabilistic, and loss characteristics needed for risk analysis.


Optimization-based scenario reduction for long-term hurricane-loss ensembles. The reduced set preserves event probabilities, inter-arrival patterns, cumulative loss distributions, and annual loss moments.


Key idea: Compact, weighted scenario ensembles can reduce computational burden while preserving the long-term hazard-loss behavior needed for regional risk assessment.

Selected publication
Wang, J., Davidson, R., & Nozick, L. (2026). An Optimization-Based Approach to Developing Computationally Efficient Long-Term Event-Loss Scenario Ensembles. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in Engineering Systems, Part A: Civil Engineering. DOI: 10.1061/AJRUA6/RUENG-2004

title: Research
text:
Exposure & Land Use
Risk evolves as development patterns change. This work couples dynamic building inventory, land-use policy, acquisition decisions, and multi-stakeholder outcomes to examine how future growth reshapes disaster risk and financial burdens.


Land-use policy strategies under different risk attitudes toward flood risk. Development is allowed to occur, but policies guide where growth takes place to limit increasing exposure.


Key idea: Land-use and acquisition strategies reduce disaster losses by redirecting growth away from higher-risk areas, especially for new construction in flood-prone locations.

Selected work
Wang, J., Williams, C., Davidson, R., Nozick, L., & Millea, M. (n.d.). Coupling Land Use Planning and Multi-Stakeholder Dynamics to Inform Disaster Risk Management: Who Pays for Risk and Who Gains from Intervention? Under review, International Journal of Disaster Risk Management.

title: Research
text:
Research Themes and Selected Work


Hazard & Loss Modeling
How can long-term hazard and loss processes be represented efficiently enough to support regional risk analysis and decision modeling?
This area develops compact, probabilistic representations of hazard events and loss sequences. The goal is to preserve the temporal, spatial, and probabilistic features that matter for risk analysis while reducing the computational burden of long simulation horizons.


Optimization-based scenario reduction for long-term hurricane-loss ensembles.


Key idea: Compact, weighted scenario ensembles make long-term hazard-loss modeling computationally tractable while preserving the features needed for policy analysis.

Selected publication
Wang, J., Davidson, R., & Nozick, L. (2026). An Optimization-Based Approach to Developing Computationally Efficient Long-Term Event-Loss Scenario Ensembles. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in Engineering Systems, Part A: Civil Engineering. DOI: 10.1061/AJRUA6/RUENG-2004


Dynamic Exposure & Land Use
How do growth, development patterns, and land-use interventions reshape future disaster risk?
This area links dynamic building inventories with land-use policy and mitigation decisions. Rather than treating exposure as fixed, the work examines how future development changes where losses occur, who bears them, and how policy can redirect growth away from higher-risk locations.


Land-use policy strategies under different risk attitudes toward flood risk.


Key idea: Land-use and acquisition strategies can reduce future losses by changing where growth occurs, especially for new construction in flood-prone areas.

Selected work
Wang, J., Williams, C., Davidson, R., Nozick, L., & Millea, M. (n.d.). Coupling Land Use Planning and Multi-Stakeholder Dynamics to Inform Disaster Risk Management: Who Pays for Risk and Who Gains from Intervention? Under review, International Journal of Disaster Risk Management.


Multi-Stakeholder Risk & Policy Dynamics
How do households, insurers, and governments respond to risk, and how do their interactions shape who bears losses and who benefits from mitigation?
This area develops computational models of coupled stakeholder behavior. It examines how mitigation funding, insurance pricing, household decisions, and public programs interact over time to shape regional risk, affordability, market outcomes, and distributional impacts.


Stakeholder-based framework linking hazard, exposure, and decision-making across households, insurers, and governments.



Policy design space illustrating how timing, spatial scale, and allocation rules shape mitigation outcomes.


Key idea: Disaster risk outcomes depend not only on hazards, but also on the structure of institutions, markets, and household decisions.

Related publications
Wang, J., Siders, A. R., Davidson, R., & Nozick, L. (2026). Stakeholder Dynamics in Disaster Mitigation Funding: The Roles of Timing, Spatial Scale and Allocation Basis in Policy Design. International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction. DOI: 10.1016/j.ijdrr.2026.106120
Davidson, R., Nozick, L., Kruse, J., Trainor, J., Millea, M., Sue Wing, I., Liu, D., Williams, C., & Wang, J. (2025). Stakeholder-based tool for the analysis of regional risk (STARR). Natural Hazards Review, 26(3), 04025031.


AI, Optimization & Decision Support
How can optimization, simulation, and AI support policy design under uncertainty?
This area uses optimization, learning-based methods, and explainable AI to evaluate policy trade-offs across risk reduction, equity, affordability, and institutional performance. The focus is on decision support tools that can connect complex simulations with interpretable policy insights.


Decision framework using direct policy search with learning and belief updating.


Key idea: AI and optimization can help identify policy designs that balance risk reduction, equity, affordability, and system-level consequences.

Related publications
Wang, J., & Johnson, D. R. (2024). Incorporating learning into direct policy search for flood risk management. Risk Analysis, 44(1), 190–202.

Recognition: Student Merit Award (Best Student Research), Engineering and Infrastructure Specialty Group, Society for Risk Analysis (2022).

Ongoing work

As a Senior Flood Engineer at Karen Clark and Company, I worked on large-scale flood model development for coastal and inland flooding across the United States.

Developed automated modeling workflows supporting large-scale U.S. flood event prediction and reproducible model development.

This work included research on hydrology and flood physics, review of historical flood events, refinement of stochastic flood catalogs, and integration of automated modeling frameworks.



Together, these efforts connect model development, policy design, and real-world implementation for disaster risk management.

title: Research
text:
Research Themes





Our research is organized around three tightly coupled components that jointly determine disaster risk outcomes:
Hazard & Loss Modeling
We develop probabilistic and computationally efficient representations of hazard events and loss processes to support long-term regional risk analysis.
Exposure & Land Use
We model how development, building inventory growth, and land-use policy reshape where risk accumulates and who is exposed.
Multi-Stakeholder Dynamics
We analyze how households, insurers, and governments respond to risk, and how their interactions shape losses, affordability, and policy outcomes.
Across these components, we use AI, optimization, and simulation to connect complex system behavior with actionable policy insights.

title: Research
text:
Selected Work


Hazard & Loss Modeling
How can long-term hazard and loss processes be represented efficiently enough to support regional risk analysis and decision modeling?
This area develops compact, probabilistic representations of hazard events and loss sequences. The goal is to preserve the temporal, spatial, and probabilistic features that matter for risk analysis while reducing the computational burden of long simulation horizons.


Optimization-based scenario reduction for long-term hurricane-loss ensembles.


Key idea: Compact, weighted scenario ensembles make long-term hazard-loss modeling computationally tractable while preserving the features needed for policy analysis.

Selected publication
Wang, J., Davidson, R., & Nozick, L. (2026). An Optimization-Based Approach to Developing Computationally Efficient Long-Term Event-Loss Scenario Ensembles. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in Engineering Systems, Part A: Civil Engineering. DOI: 10.1061/AJRUA6/RUENG-2004


Dynamic Exposure & Land Use
How do growth, development patterns, and land-use interventions reshape future disaster risk?
This area links dynamic building inventories with land-use policy and mitigation decisions. Rather than treating exposure as fixed, the work examines how future development changes where losses occur, who bears them, and how policy can redirect growth away from higher-risk locations.


Land-use policy strategies under different risk attitudes toward flood risk.


Key idea: Land-use and acquisition strategies reduce future losses by steering growth away from high-risk areas.

Selected work
Wang, J., Williams, C., Davidson, R., Nozick, L., & Millea, M. (n.d.). Coupling Land Use Planning and Multi-Stakeholder Dynamics to Inform Disaster Risk Management. Under review.


Multi-Stakeholder Risk & Policy Dynamics
How do households, insurers, and governments interact to shape risk and policy outcomes?
This area develops computational models of coupled stakeholder behavior. It examines how mitigation funding, insurance pricing, household decisions, and public programs interact over time to shape regional risk, affordability, market outcomes, and distributional impacts.


Stakeholder-based framework linking hazard, exposure, and decision-making.



Policy design space across timing, spatial scale, and allocation rules.


Key idea: Disaster outcomes depend not only on hazards, but on how institutions and decisions distribute risk.

Related publications
Wang, J., Siders, A. R., Davidson, R., & Nozick, L. (2026). Stakeholder Dynamics in Disaster Mitigation Funding. International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction.
Davidson, R., et al. (2025). STARR framework. Natural Hazards Review.


AI, Optimization & Decision Support
How can AI and optimization support policy design under uncertainty?
This area uses optimization, simulation, and learning-based methods to evaluate trade-offs across risk reduction, equity, affordability, and system performance.


Decision framework using direct policy search with learning.


Key idea: AI and optimization help identify policy designs that balance competing objectives under uncertainty.

Related publications
Wang, J., & Johnson, D. R. (2024). Direct policy search for flood risk management. Risk Analysis.

Selected Projects





Hazard & Loss Modeling
How can long-term hazard and loss processes be represented efficiently enough to support regional risk analysis and decision modeling?
This research area develops probabilistic and computationally efficient methods for representing long-term hazard and loss processes. The focus is on preserving the spatial, temporal, and probabilistic features that matter for regional risk analysis while enabling tractable large-scale simulation and decision modeling.
Selected publication
Wang, J., Davidson, R., & Nozick, L. (2026). An Optimization-Based Approach to Developing Computationally Efficient Long-Term Event-Loss Scenario Ensembles. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in Engineering Systems, Part A: Civil Engineering. DOI







Dynamic Exposure & Land Use
How do growth, development patterns, and land-use interventions reshape future disaster risk?
This research examines how development patterns, building inventory growth, and land-use policies reshape future disaster risk. Exposure is treated as dynamic rather than fixed, with emphasis on how policy can guide where growth occurs, who remains exposed, and how losses are redistributed over time.
Selected Publication
Wang, J., Williams, C., Davidson, R., Nozick, L., & Millea, M. (n.d.). Coupling Land Use Planning and Multi-Stakeholder Dynamics to Inform Disaster Risk Management. Under review.








Multi-Stakeholder Risk & Policy Dynamics
How do households, insurers, and governments interact to shape risk and policy outcomes?
This research develops computational models of how households, insurers, and governments respond to changing risk. It examines how mitigation funding, insurance pricing, household adaptation, and public programs interact to shape affordability, market outcomes, equity, and long-term risk reduction.
Selected publications

AI, Optimization & Decision Support
How can optimization, simulation, and AI support policy design under uncertainty?
This research uses optimization, simulation, learning-based methods, and explainable AI to support decision-making under deep uncertainty. The goal is to connect complex system dynamics with interpretable tools for evaluating trade-offs across risk reduction, equity, affordability, and system performance.
